Blue whiting Micromesistius poutassou exhibits a maximum recorded total length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], a size attained by the oldest and largest individuals in the northeast Atlantic stock. Females typically reach a considerably smaller total length of 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm] at the onset of puberty, marking the threshold where somatic growth begins to be complemented by gonadal investment. This length at maturation corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 23 grams [Wwp = approximately 23 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, which emerge from pelagic eggs with an average diameter of 1.16 mm, possess an initial wet weight of only 0.00082 grams [Wwb = 0.00082 grams], reflecting the limited endogenous reserves available before the onset of exogenous feeding. The pelagic larval phase is thus a critical period of rapid growth and high mortality.

Reproductive output in Blue whiting has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], mature females achieve a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 150,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 150,000 eggs per year], a value estimated from laboratory-based spawning observations. This high annual fecundity is characteristic of a batch-spawning, iteroparous strategist that produces multiple egg batches over an extended spawning season. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown female is 830 grams [Wwi = 830 grams], a mass that allows for considerable reproductive investment relative to smaller conspecifics. The relationship between body size and fecundity is strongly positive, with larger individuals contributing disproportionately to the overall egg production of the stock.

Longevity in Blue whiting is strongly modulated by ambient temperature. At a mean environmental temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the maximum lifespan is estimated at approximately 7,300 days [am = approximately 7,300 days], which equates to roughly 20 years. This extended lifespan is notable among gadoids of comparable body size and suggests a life-history strategy that balances moderate somatic growth rates with sustained, iteroparous reproductive effort over multiple decades. Field records from otolith-based ageing studies corroborate laboratory estimates, confirming that individuals can exceed two decades in age under natural conditions. The asymptotic body length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm] is typically approached only after many years of slow, indeterminate growth, with the majority of size gains occurring before the onset of sexual maturation.

The transition from pelagic larva to demersal juvenile involves a dramatic shift in both habitat and morphology. Following yolk-sac resorption, first exogenous feeding commences as the mouth opens and retinal differentiation allows for prey detection. The small initial mass at hatching, 0.00082 grams [Wwb = 0.00082 grams], means that successful recruitment depends heavily on the availability of suitable zooplankton prey during the first weeks of life. Juveniles that survive this bottleneck grow rapidly and, upon reaching a body mass of about 23 grams [Wwp = about 23 grams], begin the process of sexual maturation. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a power function, with females at puberty measuring approximately 15 cm [Lp = approximately 15 cm] in total length and weighing roughly 23 grams [Wwp = roughly 23 grams] before allocating energy toward egg production.

Comparative data with congeneric species such as southern blue whiting *Micromesistius australis* reveal that Blue whiting attains a larger ultimate body size, with females reaching 830 grams [Wwi = 830 grams] compared to the typically smaller adult masses of its southern counterpart. The maximum reproductive output at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] of approximately 150,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 150,000 eggs per year] places M. poutassou among the more fecund members of the Gadidae, a family already characterized by high fecundity. The oldest documented individuals in the northeast Atlantic have been aged at 20 years (7,300 days [am = 7,300 days]), a lifespan that supports the species' capacity for multiple spawning seasons at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. The total length at puberty of 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm] represents only about 30% of ultimate length (50 cm) [Li = 50 cm], a relatively early maturation that allows for significant post-pubertal growth and multiple reproductive events across the adult lifespan.
